q: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as _____.
e: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as chemical bonds. Intermolecular forces pull neighbouring molecules together, not atoms inside a compound. Nuclear forces hold the nucleus together, not a compound.

q: In atoms, the main shells can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells which can be filled with _____ electrons, respectively.
e: In atoms, the main shells can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells which can be filled with 2, 6, 10, and 14 electrons, respectively. A subshell is an s, p, d, or f set of orbitals inside a main shell.

q: The s subshell has only one _____ orbital.
e: The s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital. Dumbbell-shaped: a dumbbell shape is a p orbital. Double dumbbell-shaped: a dumbbell shape is a p orbital.

q: There are three _____ p orbitals ($p_x, p_y, p_z$).
e: There are three dumbbell-shaped p orbitals (px, py, pz). Spherical-shaped: a spherical orbital is s. Double dumbbell-shaped: double-dumbbell shapes belong to d orbitals.

q: The five d orbitals have _____ shapes.
e: The five d orbitals have double dumbbell shapes. A spherical orbital is s.

q: According to the _____ principle, electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones.
e: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones. Hund's rule spreads electrons through a subshell before pairing. Pauli's: pauli limits one orbital to two opposite-spin electrons.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than _____ electrons can occupy the same orbital.
e: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than two electrons can occupy the same orbital. Pauli's exclusion principle lets at most two electrons into one orbital, and those two must spin opposite ways.

q: Two electrons in the same orbital must have _____ spins.
e: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins. An orbital is a region of space where an electron is likely to be found.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is _____.
e: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is doubly occupied. Empty is not the d-subshell requirement in the transition-metal definition.

q: The electrons in the valence shells of an atom are known as the _____ electrons.
e: The electrons in the valence shells of an atom are known as the valence electrons. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its _____ in the Periodic Table.
e: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table. Period number is the shell, not the valence count. Atomic mass does not count valence electrons.

q: Atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases, which is known as the _____ rule.
e: Atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases, which is known as the octet rule. A duplet is a two-electron shell, not the usual octet. Hund's rule spreads electrons through a subshell before pairing.

q: The octet rule does not apply to _____ elements.
e: The octet rule does not apply to d-block elements. S-block is groups 1 and 2, not the transition block. P-block is groups 13 to 18.

q: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the _____ to itself.
e: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: Electron affinity is the amount of energy _____ when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
e: Electron affinity is the amount of energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom. Electron affinity is the energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron.

q: Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to _____ an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom. Ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to pull an electron off a gaseous atom.

q: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the _____ is its electronegativity.
e: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the greater is its electronegativity. Greater: ionisation energy is the energy you must put in to pull an electron off a gaseous atom.

q: There are _____ main types of chemical bonding.
e: There are three main types of chemical bonding. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by _____ forces.
e: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces. Van der Waals: intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: Among van der Waals forces, _____ forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: Among van der Waals forces, London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Most bonds are not 100% ionic or 100% covalent, instead most bonds have at least some degree of _____ character.
e: Most bonds are not 100% ionic or 100% covalent, instead most bonds have at least some degree of both ionic and covalent character. Covalent bonding is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms, and this interaction leads to the forces of attraction known as _____.
e: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms, and this interaction leads to the forces of attraction known as chemical bonds. Those outer electrons, the valence electrons, are the ones that actually form bonds.

q: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the anions. Cations form when atoms lose electrons.

q: Elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the cations. Anions form when atoms gain electrons.

q: Ionic bonding results from the _____ of electrons from one atom to another.
e: Ionic bonding results from the transfer of electrons from one atom to another. An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: Ionic bonding mostly takes place when the difference in electronegativity is greater than _____.
e: Ionic bonding mostly takes place when the difference in electronegativity is greater than 1.8.

q: Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive _____.
e: Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive non-metals. An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: When an ionic bond forms, a metal loses electrons to form positively charged ions known as _____.
e: When an ionic bond forms, a metal loses electrons to form positively charged ions known as cations. Anions form when atoms gain electrons.

q: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the _____ of that element.
e: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the valency of that element. An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: In the formation of sodium chloride, the difference in electronegativity between Na (0.9) and Cl (3.0) is _____.
e: In the formation of sodium chloride, the difference in electronegativity between Na (0.9) and Cl (3.0) is 2.1.

q: In the case of magnesium oxide, the electronegativity difference between Mg (1.2) and oxygen (3.5) is _____.
e: In the case of magnesium oxide, the electronegativity difference between Mg (1.2) and oxygen (3.5) is 2.3.

q: In general, the greater the charge on the ions, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the _____ the ionic bond will be.
e: In general, the greater the charge on the ions, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the stronger the ionic bond will be. Stronger: an ionic bond is the strong electrostatic pull between a cation and an anion after electrons transfer.

q: The melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are _____.
e: The melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are higher. Ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: In solid ionic compounds, their ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, and hence they cannot conduct _____.
e: In solid ionic compounds, their ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, and hence they cannot conduct electricity. Electricity: ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice, created by repeating _____.
e: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice, created by repeating unit cells. Unit cells: a crystal lattice is the repeating three-dimensional pattern of atoms, ions, or molecules in a solid.

q: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic, face-centred cubic, and _____ cubic.
e: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic, face-centred cubic, and body-centred cubic. A simple cubic cell has atoms only at the eight corners of the cube.

q: Sodium chloride has a cubic structure and is formed by repeating the _____ unit cell.
e: Sodium chloride has a cubic structure and is formed by repeating the face-centred cubic unit cell. A face-centred cubic cell has atoms at every corner and in the centre of each face.

q: In a sodium chloride crystal lattice, each $Na^+$ ion has _____ neighbouring $Cl^-$ ions.
e: In a sodium chloride crystal lattice, each Na+ ion has six neighbouring Cl- ions. A crystal lattice is the repeating three-dimensional pattern of atoms, ions, or molecules in a solid.

q: The term _____ number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice.
e: The term coordination number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice. A crystal lattice is the repeating 3D pattern of particles in a solid.

q: Since the coordination ratio of $Na^+$ ion to $Cl^-$ ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is _____.
e: Since the coordination ratio of Na+ ion to Cl- ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is NaCl. 6:6 reduces to 1:1, which is why the formula is NaCl.

q: A simple cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom in each _____ of the cube.
e: A simple cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom in each corner of the cube. A simple cubic cell has atoms only at the eight corners of the cube.

q: A face-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner, and an atom at the centre of each _____.
e: A face-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner, and an atom at the centre of each face. A face-centred cubic cell has atoms at every corner and in the centre of each face.

q: A body-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner and another in the _____ of the cube.
e: A body-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner and another in the centre of the cube. A body-centred cubic cell has atoms at the corners plus one atom in the middle of the cube.

q: The electrostatic attraction resulting from the opposite charges constitutes _____ bonds.
e: The electrostatic attraction resulting from the opposite charges constitutes ionic bonds. Ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: Covalent bonding usually occurs between _____.
e: Covalent bonding usually occurs between non-metals. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the _____ electrons.
e: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the shared electrons. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: When hydrogen atoms are approaching, there is a repulsive force between the electrons since like charges _____.
e: When hydrogen atoms are approaching, there is a repulsive force between the electrons since like charges repel. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: There is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the bond length where net attractive forces are _____.
e: There is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the bond length where net attractive forces are maximised. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: In single covalent bonds, only _____ pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
e: In single covalent bonds, only one pair of electrons is shared between two atoms. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: A double bond is formed by sharing _____ pairs of electrons between two atoms.
e: A double bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons between two atoms. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction and the _____ the bond length.
e: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction and the shorter the bond length. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The bond length of the single bond is the longest, followed by the double bond and _____ bond.
e: The bond length of the single bond is the longest, followed by the double bond and triple bond. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: The bond strength of the _____ bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond.
e: The bond strength of the triple bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: A coordinate bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both donated by _____ of the participating atoms.
e: A coordinate bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both donated by one of the participating atoms. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair of electrons known as a _____.
e: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair of electrons known as a lone pair. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow which indicates the direction in which the electrons are _____.
e: A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the _____ ion.
e: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the ammonium ion. A lone pair sits on an atom and is not shared in a bond, but it still takes space and can bend the shape.

q: A water molecule can react with a hydrogen ion through a coordinate bond, giving a _____ ion.
e: A water molecule can react with a hydrogen ion through a coordinate bond, giving a hydronium ion. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: Molecules with incomplete octets are called _____ molecules.
e: Molecules with incomplete octets are called electron-deficient molecules. An electron-deficient molecule does not have enough valence electrons for an octet on the central atom, like BF3.

q: An ammonia molecule can combine with boron trifluoride using a coordinate bond to form an _____.
e: An ammonia molecule can combine with boron trifluoride using a coordinate bond to form an adduct. In a coordinate, or dative, bond one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

q: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one _____ bond.
e: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one coordinate bond. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In drawing Lewis structures, for ions, it is necessary to add electrons to account for negative charges, and _____ electrons to account for positive charges.
e: In drawing Lewis structures, for ions, it is necessary to add electrons to account for negative charges, and subtract electrons to account for positive charges. A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates one.

q: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of less than _____.
e: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of less than 8. An electron-deficient molecule does not have enough valence electrons for an octet on the central atom, like BF3.

q: The central atom in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than _____.
e: The central atom in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than 8. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: The molecular shape can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, also known as the _____ model.
e: The molecular shape can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, also known as the VSEPR model. Aufbau fills lower-energy orbitals first.

q: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < _____.
e: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < lone pair-lone pair. Core-core: core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: The lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy _____ space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons.
e: The lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy more space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: A triatomic molecule ($AX_2$ type) with only two bonding pairs without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: A triatomic molecule (AX2 type) with only two bonding pairs without lone pairs has a linear shape. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, there are four bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs, hence the shape of $CO_2$ is _____.
e: In the CO2 molecule, there are four bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs, hence the shape of CO2 is linear. A bonding pair is the electron pair shared between two atoms in a covalent bond.

q: The $AX_3$ type molecule without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: The AX3 type molecule without lone pairs has a triangular planar shape. A lone pair sits on an atom and is not shared in a bond, but it still takes space and can bend the shape.

q: The $AX_2E$ type molecule, where E represents a lone pair, has a _____ shape.
e: The AX2E type molecule, where E represents a lone pair, has a bent/V-shaped shape. A lone pair sits on an atom and is not shared in a bond, but it still takes space and can bend the shape.

q: The $AX_4$ type molecule without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: The AX4 type molecule without lone pairs has a tetrahedral shape. A lone pair sits on an atom and is not shared in a bond, but it still takes space and can bend the shape.

q: The $AX_3E$ type molecule has a _____ shape.
e: The AX3E type molecule has a trigonal pyramidal shape. The direction of this chemical relationship is the one chemists actually measure.

q: In a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to _____ other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds.
e: In a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: In the case of graphite, each layer is formed with _____ rings of carbon atoms.
e: In the case of graphite, each layer is formed with hexagonal rings of carbon atoms. pH is the negative log of [H+], so a smaller pH means a more acidic solution.

q: There are weak _____ forces between the layers of graphite.
e: There are weak van der Waals forces between the layers of graphite. Van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions, including dipole-dipole, ion-dipole, and London forces.

q: In contrast to diamond, graphite has free-moving electrons in each layer, that is why graphite can conduct _____.
e: In contrast to diamond, graphite has free-moving electrons in each layer, that is why graphite can conduct electricity. pH is the negative log of [H+], so a smaller pH means a more acidic solution.

q: Silicon(IV) oxide, $SiO_2$, is an example of a giant _____ molecule.
e: Silicon(IV) oxide, SiO2, is an example of a giant covalent molecule. Covalent bonding is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: If the atoms in a covalent bond are not identical, the electrons will not be equally shared, resulting in bond _____.
e: If the atoms in a covalent bond are not identical, the electrons will not be equally shared, resulting in bond polarity. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly negative and the other atom will be slightly positive, known as a _____.
e: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly negative and the other atom will be slightly positive, known as a dipole. A dipole is a plus end and a minus end separated in space.

q: Depending on the difference in electronegativity, covalent bonds can be polar or _____.
e: Depending on the difference in electronegativity, covalent bonds can be polar or non-polar. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond _____.
e: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond increases. Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared bonding electrons toward itself.

q: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is equally attracted resulting in a _____ covalent bond.
e: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is equally attracted resulting in a non-polar covalent bond. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between atoms.

q: The degree of bond polarity is measured as a _____ of a bond.
e: The degree of bond polarity is measured as a dipole moment of a bond. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: Any non-polar covalent bond has a _____ dipole moment.
e: Any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment. In a non-polar covalent bond the two atoms share the electron pair evenly.

q: In the case of polyatomic molecules, the dipole moment of a molecule is the _____ sum of the dipole moments of various bonds.
e: In the case of polyatomic molecules, the dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of the dipole moments of various bonds. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: The $H_2O$ molecule has a bent shape and the total dipole moment is not zero, so it is a _____ molecule.
e: The H2O molecule has a bent shape and the total dipole moment is not zero, so it is a polar molecule. Dipole moment measures how polar a bond or molecule is.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel the effect of each other, thus it is a _____ molecule.
e: In the CO2 molecule, the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel the effect of each other, thus it is a non-polar molecule. A dipole is a plus end and a minus end separated in space.

q: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and _____ forces.
e: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and London dispersion forces. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two _____ molecules interact with each other in space.
e: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two dipolar molecules interact with each other in space. Dipole-dipole attraction lines up the positive end of one polar molecule with the negative end of another.

q: Ion-dipole interaction is formed from the interaction between an ion and a _____ molecule.
e: Ion-dipole interaction is formed from the interaction between an ion and a dipole molecule. Ion-dipole attraction is the pull between an ion and the charged end of a polar molecule.

q: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms as well as non-polar molecules are known as _____ forces.
e: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms as well as non-polar molecules are known as London dispersion forces. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop a _____ dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically.
e: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop a temporary dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically. A dipole is a plus end and a minus end separated in space.

q: London dispersion forces are also called induced dipole-_____ interaction.
e: London dispersion forces are also called induced dipole-induced dipole interaction. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: Due to London dispersion forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered, such as liquid nitrogen and dry ice which is solid _____.
e: Due to London dispersion forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered, such as liquid nitrogen and dry ice which is solid CO2. London dispersion forces are weak temporary-dipole attractions found in every substance.

q: The formation of hydrogen bonds requires the first molecule to have hydrogen attached to a high electronegative atom such as F, O, or _____.
e: The formation of hydrogen bonds requires the first molecule to have hydrogen attached to a high electronegative atom such as F, O, or N. A hydrogen bond is the strong intermolecular pull from H attached to N, O, or F toward another N, O, or F.

q: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction and is the _____ of all intermolecular forces.
e: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction and is the strongest of all intermolecular forces. Intermolecular forces tug neighbouring molecules or ions together; they are not the bonds inside a molecule.

q: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common _____ cloud.
e: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common electron cloud. Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell, and those are the electrons that actually form bonds.

q: These mobile electrons in metallic bonding are often described as a "sea of _____".
e: These mobile electrons in metallic bonding are often described as a "sea of electrons". Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: The positively charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by _____ electrons.
e: The positively charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by free-moving electrons. Free-moving: metallic bonding is metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms that are packed closely together in a regular arrangement called a _____.
e: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms that are packed closely together in a regular arrangement called a lattice. A crystal lattice is the repeating 3D pattern of particles in a solid.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing positive charge on the ions in the metal _____.
e: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing positive charge on the ions in the metal lattice. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the _____ size of metal ions in the lattice.
e: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the decreasing size of metal ions in the lattice. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing number of _____ electrons per atom.
e: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing number of mobile electrons per atom. Core electrons stay inner and do not bond.

q: The strength of metallic bond is _____ than that of an ionic bond.
e: The strength of metallic bond is lower than that of an ionic bond. Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal cations and a sea of delocalised electrons.

q: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become _____ compared with the ionic compounds.
e: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become lower compared with the ionic compounds. Ionic bonding is electron transfer followed by the pull between opposite ions.

q: The bonding in metals results from the interaction of the mobile electrons with the various nuclei, hence they are held together by a strong _____ attraction.
e: The bonding in metals results from the interaction of the mobile electrons with the various nuclei, hence they are held together by a strong electrostatic attraction. An ether has an oxygen between two carbon groups, C-O-C.
